## The question {.unnumbered .unlisted}

When a network trained on nothing but squared error forecasts a time series, is what it gets wrong a bias, or only the information it lacks? In laboratory experiments people overreact to the latest value of an autoregressive series, and overreact most when the series is least persistent [@afrouzi2023overreaction]. But a forecaster who has to learn the persistence ρ from the data is unbiased only on average over its prior: at any fixed ρ its estimate is pulled towards the prior, and a forecaster who sees only the last W observations is pulled harder. Part of what looks like overreaction is therefore what a rational learner does anyway. This paper builds a setting in which the right answer is known exactly, so the two can be told apart. Causal transformers are trained from scratch on simulated AR(1) series with ρ drawn from U[0, 1], at {{< var design.n_sizes >}} sizes and {{< var design.n_windows >}} memory lengths, and each is compared with the exact Bayes forecaster that has the same prior and the same window of data, called window-Bayes here.

Four terms recur. *Implied persistence* is the slope of a forecast on the current value. The *gap* is the model's implied persistence minus its benchmark's; a positive gap is overreaction beyond the benchmark. *Excess error* is the model's squared error relative to the benchmark's, in percentage points. *Window-Bayes* is the exact Bayes forecaster given only the last W observations and the time index. The rows, margins and decision rules for three hypotheses were fixed in a pre-registration tagged {{< var prereg.first_tag >}} on {{< var prereg.signoff_date >}}, before any confirmatory run; the seed is the unit of inference, and a model is *equivalent* to its benchmark when the whole {{< var design.level_pct >}}% interval of the seed mean lies inside ±{{< var design.margin.mse >}} point of excess error or ±{{< var design.margin.gap >}} of gap.

## Is the largest network Bayes? (H1) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

H1 is {{< var h1.decision >}}. With the full window, the largest model ({{< var design.size.l.layers >}} layers, width {{< var design.size.l.d >}}) is equivalent to Bayes on {{< var h1.n_equivalent >}} of {{< var h1.n_total >}} verdicts: both measures at each of the {{< var design.n_rho >}} grid values of ρ. Every interval of excess error lies between {{< var h1.mse.min_lo >}} and {{< var h1.mse.max_hi >}} points, and every interval of the gap within ±{{< var h1.gap.max_abs_end >}}. H1 is close to a replication of earlier work showing that transformers reach the optimal filter's accuracy; it adds little on its own.

## Is the window-limited network rational given its window? (H2) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

At each of W = {{< var design.windows_finite >}}, tested separately, the decision is the pre-registered wording "{{< var h2.w2.decision >}}": {{< var h2.w2.n_equivalent >}} of {{< var h2.n_total >}} verdicts are equivalent at every window (@fig-h2-gap). What the windowed network gets wrong relative to full Bayes is accounted for, within the margins, by the information it lacks. The widest interval end is {{< var h2.all.mse.widest_end >}} points of excess error and {{< var h2.all.gap.widest_end >}} of gap, both at W = {{< var h2.all.gap.widest_end_w >}} and ρ = 0. Equivalent means inside the margin, not identical: at ρ = 0 the network overstates persistence by a small amount whose interval excludes zero at every memory length (exploratory).

## Does it overreact where the matched Bayesian underreacts? (H3) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

H3 is {{< var h3.decision >}}: {{< var h3.statement >}}. At ρ = {{< var design.h3.rho_lo >}} and {{< var design.h3.rho_hi >}}, where window-Bayes underreacts against the truth and people still overreact against it, none of the {{< var h3.denominator >}} mean gaps is above zero. The null is tight: the largest upper end of a {{< var design.level_pct >}}% interval is {{< var h3.max_hi >}}, against a threshold of {{< var design.h3.threshold >}}. No finding was flagged, so the pre-registered re-training at {{< var design.steps_long >}} steps was not needed and was not run.

## What else was seen {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Exploratory: sizes s and m also match their benchmarks on all {{< var size.n_per_size >}} verdicts each. The smallest model ({{< var design.size.xs.layers >}} layer, width {{< var design.size.xs.d >}}) is "different" on {{< var size.xs.total.different >}} of {{< var size.n_per_size >}} verdicts; it pulls forecasts towards a middling persistence, which at high ρ is underreaction, the opposite of the human signature. Equivalence at the largest size arrives only at the end of training: at {{< var design.step_mid >}} of {{< var design.steps >}} steps the windowed models are equivalent on at most {{< var trace.windowed.max_equivalent_early >}} of {{< var h2.n_total >}} verdicts per window. Descriptive: when the mean and scale of the series are unknown, as they are for an experimental subject, the networks again trace their Bayes benchmarks, and a Bayesian with four observations reproduces the direction of the human curve.

## What this does not show {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The verdicts hold at step {{< var design.steps >}}, when the cosine learning rate has reached zero; they do not hold at {{< var design.step_mid >}} steps, and a different schedule or a shorter budget could leave departures that look like bias and are under-training. Window-Bayes minimises expected squared error, so a network that optimised perfectly would match it by construction: the result is about what finite training reaches, not a discovery that networks are rational. It is a result for one architecture on simulated AR(1) data, and says nothing about how a large language model or a person behaves. The human overlay does not show people overreacting beyond an information-limited Bayesian: in that setting the matched Bayesian itself overreacts at high persistence, and from ρ = {{< var overlay.first_rho_incl_w4 >}} upward the human intervals include the four-observation curve. The pre-registration is a tagged document in the author's repository, not lodged with a registry, and its tags became public only on {{< var meta.public_date >}}; three deviations ({{< var prereg.tag.v12.name >}} to {{< var prereg.tag.v14.name >}}) were fixed after confirmatory runs had started, though before the analysis code had been run on any real metrics. Exploratory, descriptive and illustrative results are not findings.
